description: We are a team from Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, working on "Abandoned but not Forgotten." Our project, Left on the Moon, is an interactive 3D website that tells the stories of equipment NASA left on the Moon and Mars, and why each piece stayed behind. Our team combines web development, UI/UX and 3D design, research and storytelling. We'd welcome members skilled in 3D modeling, animation or space history who love turning data into stories.
summary:
Left on the Moon is an interactive 3D website that tells the stories of equipment NASA left behind on the Moon and Mars, and explains why each piece stayed there. Visitors spin a 3D Moon or Mars, choose one of 11 real landing sites (Apollo 11, 12, 14, 15, 16, 17, Viking 1, Spirit, Opportunity, InSight and Ingenuity), then step onto the surface in first person. They can walk among the hardware, jump in real lunar or Martian gravity, and tap any of 40 objects to read its story, see a NASA photo and learn why it was left: weight, on purpose, a one-way trip, or a failure.

Information about these objects is scattered across technical reports that are hard for students to follow, and rarely answers the most interesting question: why was it left? Our project turns NASA's archive into a museum on another world, available in both English and Arabic, so these forgotten objects and their stories reach a wider audience.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Left on the Moon is a 3D interactive museum of the hardware NASA left on the Moon and Mars. Visitors rotate a 3D Moon or Mars, pick a landing site placed at its real coordinates, read the mission's story, then press "Stand here" to drop onto the surface in first person. Golden rings mark each object; tapping one opens a card with a NASA photo, its story and the reason it was left behind.

FEATURES

- 11 landing sites: Apollo 11, 12, 14, 15, 16, 17, Viking 1, Spirit, Opportunity, InSight and Ingenuity

- 40 real objects, from Apollo 15's Fallen Astronaut and Charlie Duke's family photo to Ingenuity's broken rotor blade

- "Why it stayed": every object is classified as left because of weight, on purpose, a one-way trip, or a failure

- First-person surface mode: walk, look around and jump with real gravity (Moon 1.62 m/s², Mars 3.71 m/s²)

- Search across all sites and objects

- Full English and Arabic versions

HOW IT WORKS

The site is built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, using the Three.js library for 3D graphics, and hosted on GitHub Pages. Planet surfaces are drawn procedurally in code, with lunar maria and craters placed at their real locations. Landing sites are converted from latitude and longitude to 3D positions. The surface terrain is generated from a height function that creates craters and rims. Walking uses the camera's viewing direction, and jumping uses real physics: each frame, gravity pulls the visitor down by the actual value of g for the Moon or Mars. Objects are selected by raycasting from the camera to the pointer.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Students, teachers and space fans get one place to explore these objects instead of scattered technical reports. Explaining why each object was left teaches real engineering trade-offs, such as how every kilogram brought home costs fuel. Arabic speakers, who rarely find space content in their language, get the full experience in Arabic.

CREATIVITY

Instead of a list or a map, visitors stand on the surface beside the hardware, like walking through a museum on another world. The "why it stayed" angle connects each object to a human or engineering decision.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

Accuracy: every object is real, and we removed any photo we could not confirm came from the right mission. Simplified 3D models and approximate positions are noted. Accessibility: high-contrast text, two languages, and motion is reduced for visitors who turn on reduced-motion settings.

USE OF AI

Our team came up with the concept, chose the content, directed the design and tested every part of the site. We used an AI assistant (Claude by Anthropic) to help us along the way: it assisted with writing and debugging the code, refining the visual layout, summarizing NASA mission information into short stories, and translating between English and Arabic. We reviewed all facts and removed anything we could not confirm. No AI-generated images are used: all photos are real NASA images, and the 3D models and planet surfaces are drawn by code.
